messages.author: ed891ef5ab438d41
messages.subject: Bayesian factor analysis
parts:
My coauthor and I are working on a governance indicators projects, and we plan to use Bayesian factor analysis to aggregate a bunch of different measures. We'd also like to use informative priors to reflect our extra-data information about the relationship between observable and latent variables.

In some detail: we have many dozens variables that measure various aspects of government capacity for a large number of countries. And we have hunches regarding the different dimensions (regulatory capacity, service delivery capacity) that these variables measure. So for instance, we might have school test scores and immunization rates, that we consider measures of service delivery; environmental regulation and business regulation, that we consider measures of regulatory capacity; and so on.

What we'd like to do is fit a factor analysis model with multiple dimensions, and encode our substantive hunches regarding which measures belong to which dimension in the priors for the discrimination parameters. But at the same time, we'd want the model to be flexible enough to allow for a given variable to load on a dimension other than the "natural" one we'd expect it to load. This is particularly important when there's some ambiguity regarding exactly what aspect of government capacity a given variable is measuring. So for instance, it is unclear whether revenue collection is more like a "service delivery" or more like regulation; and the same for clean air, and a bunch of other measures.

What I've been doing is setting the prior for the discrimination parameter of a given variable on its "natural" dimension to be centered at 1 and with a relatively small standard deviation, while the discrimination on the other dimension(s) is given a prior centered at 0 and with larger standard deviation.

So we estimate something in the form

 y[i] ~ dnorm (mu.y[i], tau.y[i])
   
mu.y[i] <- mu.0 + b[source[i],1]*theta[country[i],1] + b[source[i],2]*theta[country[i],2]+a[source[i]]

where y are the observed variables (in "long" format, so that multiple measures for a given country are stacked as successive observations in y; also, the variables are standardized so that they are all approximately on the same scale)

the theta are the latent variables (in this case, theta[ j, 1] and theta[j, 2] are the values of the latent variable for country j respectively on dimension 1 and 2) 

a[k] is the "difficulty" for observable variable k

and b the discriminations, so that b[k, l] is the discrimination parameter for observable variable k on latent dimension l. In the example, l can be either 1 or 2. 

The prior for b[k,1] is centered at one, with sd_low, if our hunch is that variable k belongs to dimension 1, and centered at 0, with sd_high, otherwise; and the same happens for the second dimension obviously.

Models like this seem to have a lot of issues with convergence, when estimated in JAGS and WinBUGS, especially if I do not set sd_high to be also quite small, and also if there are more (e.g. four) latent dimensions. Which makes me suspect that there's a problem with the model itself. It would be great if any of you here had any suggestion regarding how to design a model that allows for multiple latent dimensions while also encoding these hunches regarding which dimension a given variable belongs. [And yes, we are migrating to Stan...]

thanks
Piero

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian factor analysis
parts:
Just so you don't think I'm ignoring the message, the short
answer is "no", I don't have any suggestions, but then I don't
even know what "loading" means in this context.

Feel free to send along an implementation for comments.

Is the problem one chain stabilizing or multiple chains arriving
at the same estimates?

One thing I can say is that in Stan, unlike in BUGS or JAGS,
you need to assign a variable a value before using it. The
statements are executed in order.

Have you tried fitting simulated data to see if the sampler
can recover parameters known to generate the observed data.
You can run into sampling problems with misspecified models.

- Bob

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Bayesian factor analysis
parts:
Hi Piero

I come from the factor analysis framework in my transition to Bayesian analysis (obviously with Stan).

I would recommend you this book
http://www.amazon.com/Advanced-Bayesian-Structural-Equation-Modeling/dp/0470669527/ref=sr_1_2?ie=UTF8&qid=1405532956&sr=8-2&keywords=bayesian+structural+equation+modeling

This book shows several kinds of models, like multilevel etc. Also you can look for papers of the authors. Their code is in winbugs, but is easily translated to Stan.

Here is a Stan code example for a simple CFA of 3 corrlated factors

data{
int N; // sample size
int P; // number of variables
int D; // number of dimensions
vector[P] X[N]; // data matrix of order [N,P]
}

parameters{
vector[P] b; // intercepts
vector<lower=0>[P] lam; // factor loadings
vector[D] FS[N]; // factor scores, matrix of order [N,D]
corr_matrix[D] Rho; // correlation matrix between factors
vector<lower=0,upper=100>[P] var_p; // variance for each variable
}

transformed parameters{
vector[D] M;
vector<lower=0, upper=1000>[D] Sd_d; // sd of factors
vector[P] mu[N];
matrix[D,D] Ld;

for (m in 1:D) {
M[m] <- 0;
Sd_d[m] <- 1;}

Ld <- diag_matrix(Sd_d) * cholesky_decompose(Rho);

for(i in 1:N){
    mu[i,1] <- b[1] + lam[1]*FS[i,1];
    mu[i,2] <- b[2] + lam[2]*FS[i,1];
    mu[i,3] <- b[3] + lam[3]*FS[i,1];
    mu[i,4] <- b[4] + lam[4]*FS[i,2];
    mu[i,5] <- b[5] + lam[5]*FS[i,2];
    mu[i,6] <- b[6] + lam[6]*FS[i,2];
    mu[i,7] <- b[7] + lam[7]*FS[i,3];
    mu[i,8] <- b[8] + lam[8]*FS[i,3];
    mu[i,9] <- b[9] + lam[9]*FS[i,3];
    }
}

model{

b ~ normal(0, 100);
lam ~ normal(0.4,var_p);

for(i in 1:N){   
    X[i] ~ normal(mu[i],var_p);
    FS[i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(M, Ld);
    }

}

I didint understood what kind of model you are building, but you will need to identify the model, for example this code identify the model be setting the factors variance to 1 and the factors means to 0. There are other ways, I personally prefer this one

Hope it helps

--- Mauricio
